summary: We developed an interactive, bilingual (English / Vietnamese) astronomical image-processing and kinematic tracking web application that detects moving celestial objects—such as high-proper-motion stars, nearby brown dwarfs, and solar system bodies—from multi-epoch NASA SPHEREx and WISE observations. Addressing the challenge of extracting faint, moving sources from massive, heterogeneous sky surveys, our pipeline automates end-to-end FITS/MEF data ingestion, SPHEREx detector artifact bitmasking, WCS astrometric reprojection, PSF homogenization, and linear flux scaling. Users can visually inspect aligned exposures using a multi-epoch Blinker and difference imaging, fit linear proper-motion trajectories across observation timestamps, and validate detection completeness via synthetic Injection-Recovery simulations. This project is important because it transforms complex astronomical calibration and tracklet-linking workflows into an accessible, browser-based discovery tool—accelerating the identification of fast-moving objects in our solar neighborhood while empowering both researchers and citizen scientists to explore NASA's next-generation infrared survey data without writing custom reduction pipelines.
details:
Our project is an interactive, end-to-end astronomical image-processing and kinematic tracking web application designed to detect moving celestial objects—such as high-proper-motion stars, nearby brown dwarfs, and solar system bodies—from multi-epoch space telescope observations (NASA SPHEREx and unWISE / Legacy Survey). Instead of requiring researchers or citizen scientists to manually write complex calibration scripts for every sky coordinate, our platform automates the entire discovery workflow inside a bilingual (English / Vietnamese) web interface, guiding users from multi-epoch FITS/MEF data ingestion and exposure homogenization to visual blinking, linear trajectory fitting, and quantitative sensitivity testing.

The processing pipeline operates across four integrated stages. First, the ingestion engine loads Multi-Extension FITS (MEF) stacks, individual FITS cutouts, or live sky-coordinate queries while parsing SPHEREx detector quality bitmasks (FLAGS) to mask cosmic rays, snowballs, ghosts, optical halos, and saturated or hot pixels without discarding valid astrophysical sources. Second, because multi-epoch exposures taken across different dates and detector positions vary in pixel alignment, point-spread function (PSF) width, and background zero-points, our calibration module reprojects all frames onto a common World Coordinate System (WCS) grid with flux conservation, measures per-epoch FWHM to convolve images to a uniform PSF resolution, and linearly scales fluxes so stationary background stars subtract cleanly. Third, users can inspect aligned time-series exposures through an interactive Blinker featuring adjustable playback speeds, multiple astronomical stretch modes (asinh, log, linear, zscale), and difference-image overlays. Finally, the tracking engine detects candidate sources at each observation timestamp (MJD-OBS) using DAOStarFinder, links consistent linear trajectories across epochs to measure proper motion ($\mu_\alpha \cos\delta$, $\mu_\delta$), and runs an Injection-Recovery simulation that injects synthetic moving stars across varying magnitudes and velocities to quantify detection completeness.

By automating calibration, PSF-matched differencing, and tracklet linking, the project significantly lowers the technical barrier to analyzing massive all-sky survey datasets and accelerates the discovery of faint, fast-moving neighbors in the solar vicinity. Pairing rigorous astrophysics algorithms with an accessible bilingual UI and exportable CSV catalogs and diagnostic plots also democratizes space telescope data for students and citizen scientists. Furthermore, to ensure uninterrupted reliability during live archive outages, we designed the system to support both online survey queries and pre-loaded or user-uploaded FITS/MEF datasets; because NASA's IRSA TAP service experienced downtime during the submission window, we bundled a real multi-epoch SPHEREx MEF dataset directly into the repository so the entire pipeline runs out of the box.

We built the application entirely in Python 3, leveraging core open-source scientific and astronomical libraries including Astropy (WCS transformations, FITS/MEF I/O, coordinate handling, and kernel convolution), Photutils (PSF/FWHM estimation and DAOStarFinder photometry), and Reproject (flux-conserving astrometric alignment), alongside NumPy, SciPy, and Pandas for numerical computing and catalog management. The interactive front end and visual diagnostics are powered by Streamlit and Matplotlib, interfacing with data products from NASA/IPAC IRSA (SPHEREx) and Legacy Survey / unWISE.

The creativity of our approach lies in uniting a classic astronomical discovery method—the Blink Comparator famously used to discover Pluto—with modern automated PSF-matched difference imaging and real-time Injection-Recovery completeness curves inside a single browser-based workspace. Throughout development, our team carefully accounted for key observational and engineering constraints, including temporal baseline differences between newly collected SPHEREx exposures and archival multi-year WISE baselines, false-positive suppression against single-frame detector transients, and multi-threaded caching to keep interactive processing responsive in a web environment.
